title: Gulf of Tonkin
subtitle: A real first engagement, a phantom second attack, and a certainty the evidence did not support
livingFileNotice: This is a Living Evidence File. It records the assessment of available evidence at the date shown. Newly declassified records from NSA, State Department, or the LBJ Library bearing on the 2–4 August 1964 chronology, or material historiographical findings about the SIGINT record, will enter the private dossier first and then this file with a visible changelog entry. If later evidence weakens any current finding, this file will say so.

overall.label: Real engagement on 2 August; public representation of 4 August exceeded the evidence
overall.summary: On 2 August 1964, USS Maddox was involved in a real engagement with North Vietnamese patrol craft in the Gulf of Tonkin. That engagement is supported by naval records, the State Department's Foreign Relations of the United States documentary series (FRUS 1964–68, Volume I, Document 255), and NSA historian Robert J. Hanyok's official SIGINT reconstruction. On 4 August, confused radar, sonar and intelligence reporting produced reports of a second attack while the on-scene commander was simultaneously transmitting serious doubt: Captain John Herrick's message 041727Z, received in Washington at approximately 1:27 p.m., said that many reported contacts and torpedoes fired 'appear doubtful,' that 'freak weather effects' on radar and 'over-eager' sonarmen may have accounted for many reports, and that no visual sightings had been made. An airborne observer — Admiral James Stockdale — reported seeing no enemy boats, no wakes, no torpedo tracks, and no boat impacts. Despite this, a Pentagon meeting at 4:47 p.m. on 4 August, acknowledging the lack of 'a clear and convincing showing that an attack on the destroyers had in fact occurred,' concluded that an attack had taken place. That evening, President Johnson publicly described the event as a second 'renewed hostile attack' and ordered retaliatory air strikes. Congress was briefed under the dual-attack narrative and passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (PL 88-408) on 7 August. Hanyok's classified study, written in 2000–2001 and declassified in November 2005, concluded from the full SIGINT archive — including intercepts not included in the contemporaneous public reporting — that 'the overwhelming body of reports, if used, would have told the story that no attack had happened,' that 'a conscious effort ensued to demonstrate that the attack occurred,' and that what was issued in the Gulf of Tonkin SIGINT summaries beginning late on 4 August 'was deliberately skewed to support the notion that there had been an attack.' That establishes a serious failure of evidence, intelligence reporting, and public representation. It does not establish that every senior official personally knew in real time that no attack had occurred and knowingly deceived Congress. The distinction matters: contemporaneous fog-of-war, motivated certainty under acknowledged thin evidence, and selective SIGINT packaging can produce a false public narrative without requiring that every principal was a deliberate liar at the moment of speaking. The personal-intent question — what LBJ and McNamara actually knew at the moment of the public address — remains an open residual at POSSIBLE–PROBABLE. This case belongs beside Operation Northwoods methodologically: where Northwoods documented institutional willingness to plan public deception (on paper, not executed), Gulf of Tonkin documents a real event whose public representation substantially outran the available evidence and whose intelligence reporting was skewed toward a predetermined narrative.

claims.claim: On 2 August 1964, USS Maddox was involved in a real military engagement with North Vietnamese patrol craft in the Gulf of Tonkin. At approximately 3:40 a.m. EDT, Maddox reported high-speed craft with apparent intent of torpedo attack; 27 minutes later it reported being under attack by three North Vietnamese patrol craft. Aircraft from USS Ticonderoga assisted in repelling the attack, and one North Vietnamese craft was reported damaged. This engagement is supported by multiple independent evidence paths: the FRUS 1964–68 documentary record, NSA historian Hanyok's SIGINT reconstruction (which confirms the 2 August engagement occurred), and subsequent historiography including North Vietnamese acknowledgments of the first-day combat. The 2 August engagement occurred in the context of DESOTO electronic intelligence patrols and OPLAN 34A South Vietnamese commando raids against North Vietnamese coastal installations; this context complicates the 'unprovoked' framing used in public statements but does not erase or diminish the real combat that took place. The 2 August engagement is not in dispute. It must appear near the top of any honest account of this case.
claims.why: FRUS 1964–68 Volume I, Document 255 (Editorial Note) documents the Maddox engagement chronology at the State Department's official documentary level. Hanyok's NSA cryptologic history explicitly confirms the 2 August attack occurred while his study focuses its critical reconstruction on the 4 August events. The 2 August engagement is accepted across the historiographical spectrum — including historians who strongly dispute the 4 August narrative. Confidence is Very high because multiple independent primary paths converge without contrary evidence challenging the basic fact of combat on 2 August.

claims.claim: The second North Vietnamese attack publicly described on 4 August 1964 did not occur as represented. No North Vietnamese naval forces attacked USS Maddox and USS Turner Joy that night. The public narrative — of a second 'renewed hostile attack' on US ships in international waters — was not supported by the full available evidence and has not been vindicated by the declassified record. This finding rests on three independent converging paths: (1) NSA historian Hanyok's reconstruction from the complete SIGINT archive, which found that 'the overwhelming body of reports, if used, would have told the story that no attack had happened' and that North Vietnamese naval forces on the night of 4 August were engaged in salvage operations following the 2 August combat, not attacking US ships; (2) Captain Herrick's contemporaneous command doubt, expressed in message 041727Z (received in Washington approximately 1:27 p.m. on 4 August), stating that reported contacts and torpedoes fired 'appear doubtful' and recommending a 'complete evaluation before any further action'; and (3) the negative airborne visual report from Admiral James Stockdale, who was flying overhead and reported no enemy boats, no wakes, no torpedo tracks, and no boat impacts. The absence of debris, wreckage, or visual confirmation of any North Vietnamese craft that night further supports this conclusion. This claim is stated at its defensible scope: 'no attack as publicly described.' It does not claim omniscience about every radar contact or sonar ping that night, or that field operators were consciously fabricating reports. Those operators experienced genuinely confusing conditions — darkness, weather, radar interference, operator stress, and bleed-over SIGINT from the 2 August engagement. The claim is that no North Vietnamese attack on the destroyers occurred that night, as Hanyok's full-SIGINT reconstruction concludes.
claims.why: Hanyok, writing from access to the full NSA SIGINT archive, reached the conclusion on page 49 of his study that no attack had happened and that a 'conscious effort ensued to demonstrate that the attack occurred.' His language about products being 'deliberately skewed to support the notion that there had been an attack' is the strongest phrase in the official record and is attributed at the SIGINT reporting process level. The Herrick cable (FRUS d276) is contemporaneous command-level doubt from the on-scene commander transmitted the same afternoon, before the public address. Stockdale's negative visual report adds an independent physical-observation path. These three paths converge. The main limitations: Hanyok is one NSA official historian whose full archive access cannot be independently replicated by outside researchers; the original Vietnamese-language texts of critical 4 August intercepts are missing from NSA archives (Hanyok notes this), meaning his translation and interpretation of key SIGINT cannot be externally verified in detail. These limitations justify noting the evidence base carefully without abandoning the KNOWN verdict, which is supported by the convergence of official SIGINT history, contemporaneous command doubt, and negative visual observation.

claims.claim: President Johnson publicly described the 4 August event as a 'renewed hostile attack' and 'repeated' aggression against US ships before the underlying uncertainty was resolved. In his 4 August 1964 radio and television address, Johnson stated that 'renewed hostile actions against United States ships on the high seas' had occurred and that 'the initial attack on the destroyer Maddox, on August 2, was repeated today by a number of hostile vessels attacking two U.S. destroyers with torpedoes.' In his 5 August message to Congress he stated that 'the North Vietnamese regime had conducted further deliberate attacks against U.S. naval vessels operating in international waters.' This public certainty was delivered after Herrick's 'appear doubtful' cable had been received in Washington (approximately 1:27 p.m. on 4 August) and after a Pentagon meeting at 4:47 p.m. had acknowledged the 'lack of a clear and convincing showing that an attack on the destroyers had in fact occurred' while still concluding that an attack had taken place. The gap between internal uncertainty and public certainty is a KNOWN process finding, established by comparing the chronology of the Herrick cable and the 4:47 p.m. meeting (both in FRUS d276) against the timing and language of the public address. At the 4 August NSC meeting, USIA Director Carl Rowan asked 'do we know for a fact that the North Vietnamese provocation took place?' and McNamara responded that 'we will know definitely in the morning' — indicating that certainty was not established at the time of the public certainty claim.
claims.why: The public addresses are primary documents (UCSB Presidency Project; Avalon Project). Their wording is unambiguous: 'repeated today... with torpedoes'; 'further deliberate attacks.' FRUS d276 provides the contemporaneous Washington chronology with timestamps: Herrick's cable at 1:27 p.m.; the 4:47 p.m. meeting; the public address that evening. FRUS d278 records the NSC meeting including Rowan's question and McNamara's 'we will know definitely in the morning.' The juxtaposition of these documents establishes that the public certainty statement was made after significant internal doubt had been expressed and before that doubt was resolved. The claim does not require that every principal was knowingly lying — that is the separate personal-intent question addressed in C5.

claims.claim: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (PL 88-408, H.J. Res. 1145, approved 7 August 1964) was passed by Congress under the dual-attack narrative after congressional leaders were briefed on 4 August. The Resolution declared that 'Congress approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression' and included a Southeast Asia collective defence clause. It passed 416–0 in the House and 88–2 in the Senate, with Senators Morse and Gruening dissenting. The Resolution was subsequently used as the primary statutory authority for massively expanded US military operations in Southeast Asia. Congress repealed it in January 1971 (P.L. 91-672). The fact that a draft resolution language had been prepared by William Bundy and Far Eastern Affairs in June 1964 — two months before the August events — establishes that the administration had pre-existing desire for broad Southeast Asia authority; it does not resolve whether the 4 August incident was invented or exploited. The Tonkin Gulf Resolution is the policy product of a process that used a public certainty claim the evidence did not support. What the Resolution's text specifically authorised — repelling attacks and preventing further aggression — is narrower than the blank-check characterisation sometimes applied to it; its scope in practice was expanded through executive war-powers theory.
claims.why: The Resolution text is a primary document available from NARA milestone documents. FRUS d280 records the 4 August leadership meeting at which congressional leaders were briefed under the dual-attack framing. Hanyok p.46 documents the pre-existing June 1964 draft resolution, which is process evidence about the administration's pre-existing authority desires. The pre-drafted resolution is cited as motive context; it is not itself proof that the 4 August incident was manufactured — as Hanyok notes, Johnson declined to use a similar September 1964 DESOTO scare for further escalation, showing that the August incident's specific character still mattered for the political franchise. The resolution's repeal in 1971 (referenced in public record and NARA) is cited as historical closure.

claims.claim: SIGINT reporting on the night of 4 August was selectively packaged in ways that supported the second-attack narrative beyond what the full body of intercepts justified. Hanyok's reconstruction concluded on page 49 that 'the overwhelming body of reports, if used, would have told the story that no attack had happened,' that 'a conscious effort ensued to demonstrate that the attack occurred,' and that what was issued in the Gulf of Tonkin SIGINT summaries beginning late on 4 August 'was deliberately skewed to support the notion that there had been an attack.' The scope of this finding is the SIGINT reporting and crisis-centre process — the analysts and reporting chain within NSA who produced the SIGINT products during the crisis. It is not established that this selective packaging resulted from explicit direction by senior policymakers or was a top-down administration-wide plan. Hanyok himself notes there is no 'smoking gun' memorandum establishing a command-level fabrication order, and that 'why this happened' at the actor level remains uncertain. The claim is therefore rated PROBABLE–KNOWN (recorded as PROBABLE at the high end) rather than KNOWN, because: the actor level and precise mechanism of the selective packaging are not fully established by the evidence; Hanyok's 'deliberately skewed' and 'conscious effort' language applies to the SIGINT reporting chain, and upgrading this to a finding about senior political leadership or the Oval Office would outrun the available evidence. The claim does not collapse into the weaker 'analysts were just confused' position: Hanyok's language is explicit that the selectivity was not merely accidental. But the scope is the reporting process, not proved to be the president's office.
claims.why: Hanyok p.49 is the primary load-bearing source. The NSA Archive EBB 132 press release (1 December 2005) quotes Hanyok's conclusion that there was no second attack and that SIGINT 'fit the claim.' These are strong findings from an official SIGINT historian with full archive access. The limitation: Hanyok is one official history written twenty years after the events; the original Vietnamese-language texts of critical intercepts are missing from the archive (Hanyok notes this), meaning exact translation cannot be independently verified; and Hanyok's 'why' for the skewing — the actor-level question — remains unresolved even within his own study. The independence limitation (one primary official historian for the core SIGINT packaging finding) justifies PROBABLE over KNOWN. The adversarial test: a SIGINT historian would note that crisis-centre analytic culture, confirmation bias, and institutional momentum can produce selective products without explicit direction — that reading is consistent with Hanyok's 'why remains unknown' language and must remain in view.

claims.claim: The question of whether LBJ or McNamara personally knew at the moment of the 4 August public address and congressional briefings that no second attack had occurred, and made their public statements knowingly, cannot be resolved on available evidence. This proposition is assessed at POSSIBLE–PROBABLE as a residual (recorded as POSSIBLE at the upper end of that range). The circumstantial case: Herrick's 'appear doubtful' cable was received in Washington approximately 1:27 p.m. on 4 August; the 4:47 p.m. Pentagon meeting language explicitly acknowledged 'lack of a clear and convincing showing'; both events preceded the public address. Policy motive was evident (pre-drafted resolution, escalation desire). The 'flying fish' comment attributed to Johnson days after the incident (Hanyok p.47) shows post-crisis private doubt, not a same-night confession. The case against: the 4:47 p.m. meeting still concluded that an attack had taken place, listing five supporting factors. McNamara's memoir treated the evidence as still 'convincing' decades later (Hanyok p.1 note 3). The fog-of-war and crisis-pressure environment meant that principals acting in good faith on the best available evidence — while that evidence was selectively packaged — could have reached genuine if wrong conclusions. No contemporaneous document records LBJ or McNamara saying, in effect, 'I know this didn't happen and I'm going to say it did.' The distinction between this proposition and C3 (public certainty exceeded the evidence) matters: C3 is KNOWN because the gap between internal uncertainty and public certainty is documented; C6 is the finer question of deliberate personal knowledge of falsehood, which requires evidence of state of mind at the moment of statement that the record does not provide.
claims.why: The honest assessment of what Herrick's cable timing, the 4:47 p.m. meeting, and the 'flying fish' post-crisis remark establish is that: doubt was available before the speech; the meeting under thin evidence still concluded an attack; and Johnson later privately expressed scepticism. Together these justify POSSIBLE–PROBABLE but not PROBABLE or KNOWN. McNamara's memoir treating the evidence as 'convincing' is the strongest adverse indicator — a man who published a book taking moral responsibility for the war's escalation still did not, in that memoir, say 'I knew on 4 August it hadn't happened.' Absence of a confession is not proof of sincere belief; but the combination of contrary memoir evidence plus the fog-of-war environment and the fact that the 4:47 pm meeting listed five specific factors for their conclusion means this cannot be upgraded without a contemporaneous document establishing knowledge of the falsehood at the moment of the public statement.

claims.claim: The Northwoods–Tonkin method pair establishes two distinct cases that together update the prior about institutional capability and behaviour: (1) Northwoods (1962) documents formal JCS-level planning for public deception operations against Cuba — proposals not executed as an authorised campaign; (2) Gulf of Tonkin (1964) documents a real first engagement followed by a second night whose public representation substantially outran the evidence and whose intelligence reporting was skewed toward the attack narrative. Together they establish that: (a) US military and government institutions formally contemplated public deception; (b) the translation of an uncertain situation into public certainty, for policy purposes, is historically documented. They do not establish: that every later contested event used the same mechanism; that the Tonkin outcome was planned in advance as a pure fabrication; or that Northwoods was the template for Tonkin. Each later case requires its own evidence. The Tonkin case specifically refutes the strongest simplification: 'the 2 August engagement was also fake.' It was not. The correct lesson from the Northwoods–Tonkin pair is that public deception can be formally planned, and that a real event can be publicly represented with certainty that the underlying evidence did not support — without these findings proving anything about any subsequent alleged false flag.
claims.why: C7 is a methodological synthesis drawing on C1–C6. The method pair has explicit architectural purpose in Chapter 4 of the Ministry's outline: Northwoods is the unexecuted planned pretext; Tonkin is the sold second night that wasn't. The anti-slide rule is the load-bearing methodological lesson: neither document licenses inventing evidence about any other event. This claim is KNOWN because the proposition is about what the two documented cases do and do not establish — a logical/methodological claim with clear support, not a contested factual claim requiring further primary evidence.

timeline.event: A draft resolution providing broad Southeast Asia authority is prepared by William Bundy (Assistant Secretary for Far Eastern Affairs) and State Department colleagues, two months before the August incidents. The draft is shelved pending an opportunity. Hanyok p.46 documents this pre-existing legislative desire.
timeline.effect: Establishes that the administration wanted broad Southeast Asia authority before August — relevant as motive context but not itself proof that the August incident was manufactured

timeline.event: South Vietnamese commandos, under OPLAN 34A, conduct raids on North Vietnamese coastal installations at Hon Me and Hon Ngu. USS Maddox is conducting DESOTO electronic intelligence patrols in the same area. North Vietnam may have interpreted the Maddox as connected to or supporting the commando raids.
timeline.effect: Context for North Vietnamese motivation for the 2 August engagement; complicates 'unprovoked' framing; does not erase or diminish the real 2 August combat

timeline.event: USS Maddox is attacked by three North Vietnamese torpedo boats in the Gulf of Tonkin. At approximately 3:40 a.m. EDT, Maddox reports high-speed craft with apparent intent of torpedo attack; 27 minutes later reports attack underway. Aircraft from USS Ticonderoga assist. One North Vietnamese craft is reported damaged. The engagement is confirmed by multiple independent evidence paths. North Vietnamese naval forces acknowledged the first-day combat in later historiography.
timeline.effect: A real military engagement. KNOWN. Must not be erased by the 4 August controversy. The 2 August engagement provided the political and military backdrop for the disputed 4 August reports.

timeline.event: USS Maddox and USS Turner Joy begin reporting contacts in the Gulf of Tonkin. In conditions of darkness, rough weather, heavy sea state, and radar/sonar interference, crew members report what they believe are torpedo attacks, boat wakes, and hostile fire. 27 separate radar contacts are reported. No enemy craft are visually confirmed. Admiral James Stockdale, flying overhead in an A-1 Skyraider, sees 'no boats, no boat wakes, no ricochets off boats, no boat impacts, no torpedo wakes — nothing but black sea and American firepower.' Hanyok's full-SIGINT reconstruction would later conclude that North Vietnamese forces on this night were conducting salvage operations following the 2 August combat, not attacking US ships.
timeline.effect: The chaotic night whose reporting became the justification for the Resolution. Real-time conditions produced genuine confusion among field operators; this fog-of-war does not itself explain the later selective SIGINT packaging or the public certainty claim.

timeline.event: Captain John Herrick's message 041727Z is received in Washington. It states: 'Review of action makes many reported contacts and torpedoes fired appear doubtful. Freak weather effects on radar and over-eager sonarmen may have accounted for many reports. No visual sightings by Maddox. Suggest complete evaluation before any further action.' FRUS 1964–68 Volume I, Document 276 documents this chronology.
timeline.effect: The on-scene commander's same-day doubt, received in Washington before the public address and before the 4:47 p.m. Pentagon meeting. This is the load-bearing evidence that uncertainty was known in Washington before public certainty was claimed.

timeline.event: Secretary of Defense McNamara, Deputy Secretary Vance, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff meet 'to marshal the evidence to overcome lack of a clear and convincing showing that an attack on the destroyers had in fact occurred.' They conclude that an attack had taken place, listing five factors: illumination and automatic weapons fire; a report of cockpit lights; identification of vessel PGM 142 and its engagement with a US aircraft; a North Vietnamese radio announcement reporting their boats had been 'sacrificed'; and Admiral Sharp's determination. FRUS d276 documents this meeting.
timeline.effect: The moment at which the administration moved from acknowledged uncertainty to concluded certainty. The 'marshal the evidence' language is the strongest process-level record of motivated certainty under thin evidence. It precedes the public address that evening.

timeline.event: President Johnson delivers a radio and television address to the American people stating that 'renewed hostile actions against United States ships on the high seas' have occurred and that 'the initial attack on the destroyer Maddox, on August 2, was repeated today by a number of hostile vessels attacking two U.S. destroyers with torpedoes.' He announces retaliatory air strikes and states he will seek a congressional resolution. At the NSC meeting (FRUS d278), USIA Director Carl Rowan had asked 'do we know for a fact that the North Vietnamese provocation took place?' McNamara responded 'we will know definitely in the morning.'
timeline.effect: The public certainty claim, delivered after Herrick's doubt cable and after the 4:47 pm meeting acknowledged thin evidence. The gap between internal uncertainty and public statement is a KNOWN process finding.

timeline.event: President Johnson sends a message to Congress stating that 'the North Vietnamese regime had conducted further deliberate attacks against U.S. naval vessels operating in international waters' and requests the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution. US Navy aircraft conduct retaliatory air strikes on North Vietnamese naval facilities. Congressional leaders are briefed under the dual-attack narrative (FRUS d280).
timeline.effect: The administration's formal congressional case for the Resolution, built on the 4 August dual-attack narrative

timeline.event: Congress passes the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (PL 88-408, H.J. Res. 1145) 416–0 in the House and 88–2 in the Senate, with Senators Wayne Morse and Ernest Gruening dissenting. The Resolution declares that Congress 'approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression' and includes a clause on Southeast Asia collective defence.
timeline.effect: The legislative product of the crisis. Becomes the statutory authority cited for massively expanded US military operations in Southeast Asia over the following years.

timeline.event: The Johnson administration uses the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution as authority for escalating military commitment in Vietnam. The resolution is cited as the legal basis for troop deployments that would eventually reach over 500,000. The 'unprovoked attack' framing is used to build and maintain domestic political support. President Johnson makes a private remark within days of the incident — documented by Hanyok p.47 — about 'those damn stupid sailors just shooting at flying fish,' indicating post-crisis private doubt about the 4 August events.
timeline.effect: The policy legacy of the incidents; the 'flying fish' remark is post-crisis private doubt, not a same-night confession of knowing deception

timeline.event: NSA historian Robert J. Hanyok writes 'Skunks, Bogies, Silent Hounds, and the Flying Fish: The Gulf of Tonkin Mystery, 2–4 August 1964' for the NSA's Cryptologic Quarterly (Winter 2000/Spring 2001). Working from the full NSA SIGINT archive — including documents not previously available to researchers — Hanyok concludes that no second attack occurred on 4 August and that SIGINT reporting was selectively packaged toward the attack narrative.
timeline.effect: The primary official SIGINT reconstruction, written from full archive access. Classified at time of writing; declassification exposes the internal NSA record on what SIGINT actually showed.

timeline.event: Hanyok's study is declassified under a FOIA request (case #43933) and released publicly. The National Security Archive (EBB 132, 1 December 2005 press release) publishes the study alongside over 140 previously classified NSA documents and highlights Hanyok's conclusion: 'there was no second attack on U.S. ships in Tonkin on August 4, 1964' and that SIGINT 'fit the claim.'
timeline.effect: The official SIGINT verdict on the 4 August events enters the public record. The NSA Archive's EBB 132 collection is the stable inspection path for Hanyok's study (National Security Archive copy) and supporting documents.

timeline.event: Congress repeals the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (P.L. 91-672), terminating it as statutory authority for US military operations in Southeast Asia.
timeline.effect: Legislative closure on the Resolution's formal authority, by which point US forces were already withdrawing under the Nixon administration

hypotheses.title: Both 2 August and 4 August attacks occurred as publicly represented
hypotheses.status: Rejected for 4 August; supported for 2 August
hypotheses.text: Both incidents involved real North Vietnamese naval attacks on US destroyers as publicly described. The 2 August attack was real and unprovoked; the 4 August attack was also real and deliberate.
hypotheses.test: This predicts: visual confirmation of enemy craft on 4 August; SIGINT indicating attack rather than salvage; surviving physical evidence of torpedo tracks or boat impacts; absence of contemporaneous command doubt; North Vietnamese accounts of a 4 August attack. None of these hold for the 4 August element. No visual confirmation; Hanyok's full-SIGINT reconstruction finds no attack; command-level doubt expressed same day; North Vietnamese accounts in later historiography do not confirm a 4 August attack. The 2 August element of this hypothesis is strongly supported. The 4 August element is rejected by the available evidence.

hypotheses.title: 2 August engagement was real; 4 August was a phantom created by confused reporting
hypotheses.text: The 2 August attack on USS Maddox occurred and is documented. On 4 August, genuine operational confusion — darkness, weather, radar and sonar interference, over-eager operators, psychological stress after the 2 August engagement — produced false reports of a second attack where none occurred. The North Vietnamese navy was conducting salvage operations, not attacking US ships.
hypotheses.test: This predicts: documented real combat on 2 August (confirmed, C1); contemporaneous command doubt on 4 August (confirmed, Herrick 041727Z); negative visual observation from airborne platform (confirmed, Stockdale); SIGINT reconstruction pointing to non-attack (confirmed, Hanyok); absence of physical evidence of attack on 4 August (confirmed). All predictions hold. The question H-one-attack leaves open is the process question: was the confused reporting purely fog-of-war, or was there active selection pressure on what SIGINT reached decision makers?

hypotheses.title: Honest real-time error only: no narrative pressure or selective packaging
hypotheses.status: Incomplete — consistent with object-level finding but does not explain packaging
hypotheses.text: Policymakers dealt with honest but confused operational reports and made a rapid error under crisis conditions. Principals genuinely believed an attack had occurred. The public certainty claim was an honest error, not a product of motivated certainty or selective intelligence packaging.
hypotheses.test: This predicts: no evidence of selective SIGINT packaging; no acknowledgement of uncertainty before public statement; principals consistently treating the 4 August reports as certain. Two predictions fail: FRUS d276 records the 4:47 p.m. meeting explicitly acknowledging 'lack of a clear and convincing showing' before concluding an attack occurred; Hanyok's reconstruction finds that SIGINT products withheld 'the overwhelming body of reports' that contradicted the attack narrative. H-fog-only is an incomplete explanation: it accounts for genuine field-operator confusion but cannot explain the selective SIGINT product or the public certainty asserted after doubt was on the table.

hypotheses.title: Policy preference and motivated certainty shaped use of shaky evidence
hypotheses.text: The administration's policy preference for a congressional resolution and escalation authority shaped how uncertain reports were interpreted and how the public narrative was constructed. Principals chose certainty under acknowledged thin evidence, producing a public account more definite than the intelligence warranted.
hypotheses.test: This predicts: pre-existing desire for authority before the incident (confirmed, June draft resolution); explicit acknowledgement of thin evidence before reaching the certainty conclusion (confirmed, 'marshal the evidence' language); selective SIGINT products that emphasised attack-consistent intercepts while omitting the broader body (confirmed, Hanyok p.49); public statements more certain than the internal record. All predictions hold. H-motivated operates at the process level and is compatible with H-fog-only at the field level: field operators were genuinely confused; the reporting chain produced selectively packaged products; the Washington meeting marshalled evidence under thin foundations; the public address stated certainty.

hypotheses.title: Senior officials deliberately fabricated the entire 4 August incident from scratch
hypotheses.status: Not supported at the personal-knowing-lie level
hypotheses.text: LBJ, McNamara, and other senior officials personally knew in real time that no attack had occurred and deliberately fabricated the public account — not out of fog-of-war or motivated certainty, but as a knowing, intentional lie.
hypotheses.test: This predicts: contemporaneous documentation of officials stating they knew no attack occurred; active fabrication of field reports; clear evidence of top-down direction to produce false SIGINT products. None of these hold at the available evidence level. The 4:47 p.m. meeting concluded that an attack had occurred, listing five factors — not 'we know this didn't happen.' McNamara's memoir (decades after the events) still treated the evidence as 'convincing.' Hanyok finds no 'smoking gun' memorandum establishing top-down fabrication orders. H-deliberate-fabrication at the full personal-knowing-lie level remains POSSIBLE–PROBABLE as a residual, not established. What is established is that public certainty substantially outran the evidence and that SIGINT reporting was selectively packaged — these findings are consistent with motivated certainty, institutional momentum, and selective reporting without requiring that every principal was a deliberate liar at the moment of speaking.

independence: 2 August action record (tonkin-2aug-action): USS Maddox ship reports and tactical record for the 2 August engagement. The primary direct-evidence path for C1. FRUS d255 is the State Department documentary record of this chronology.

FRUS 1964–68 Volume I (frus-1964-v01): The State Department's Foreign Relations of the United States documentary edition covering the 2–5 August 1964 period. Documents 255 (2 August engagement note), 276 (4 August chronology, Herrick cable, 4:47 p.m. meeting), 278 (NSC meeting), and 280 (congressional leadership briefing) provide the Washington-level chronology as an independent evidential path from the SIGINT history. These are edited diplomatic/policy documents, not raw cables, but they represent the official documentary record.

NSA Hanyok SIGINT history (nsa-hanyok-2001/2005): Robert J. Hanyok's NSA cryptologic history, written from full NSA archive access. The primary source for the full-SIGINT reconstruction of 4 August (C2), and for the SIGINT packaging findings (C5). The most direct official reconstruction from inside the intelligence record. Limitation: one official history not independently replicated by a researcher with equivalent archive access.

Herrick contemporaneous doubt (tonkin-herrick-4aug): Captain Herrick's message 041727Z, documented through FRUS d276. An independent path from Hanyok: a contemporaneous field-commander record expressing doubt the same afternoon, before any historical reconstruction. This is contemporaneous primary evidence of command-level uncertainty, independent of Hanyok's later reconstruction.

Airborne negative visual (hanyok-stockdale-air): Admiral Stockdale's negative visual observation from his airborne platform on the night of 4 August, as documented in Hanyok's study (p.1, citing Stockdale memoir path). An independent physical-observation path from the SIGINT record and field radar/sonar reports. Limitation: this path is conveyed through Hanyok's citation of Stockdale's memoir, not from a direct primary military report independently accessed in this research pass.

LBJ public statements (lbj-public-aug1964): The primary documentary record of the public certainty claim — the 4 August radio/television address (UCSB Presidency Project) and 5 August message to Congress (Avalon Project). Independent of the SIGINT and field-command paths; establishes the precise language and timing of the public narrative.
Resolution statutory text (pl-88-408): PL 88-408 as a primary statutory product. The documentary record of the legislative outcome, independent of executive-branch materials.

US Navy official contrary history (s-marolda-fitzgerald): Marolda and Fitzgerald's US Navy official history (1986), which treated the second-attack evidence as conclusive. A partially contrary institutional lineage — the Navy's own official history did not adopt the Hanyok conclusion. This is important for independence accounting: it shows that official historiography was not monolithic on the 4 August question.

McNamara participant memoir (s-mcnamara-memoir): McNamara's In Retrospect (1995), in which he still treated the evidence for the second attack as 'convincing' while taking moral responsibility for the war's escalation. A contrary participant-memory path: the Secretary of Defense who was centrally involved did not, in his memoir, say he knew the second attack had not occurred.

Pre-Hanyok critical reconstruction (s-moise-1996): Edwin Moïse's Tonkin Gulf and the Escalation of the Vietnam War (University of North Carolina Press, 1996), written before Hanyok's study was declassified. An independent academic reconstruction from publicly available sources. A full deep-read of this monograph remains an open residual in this research pass; Moïse provides an independent secondary historiographical path.
openQuestions: The original Vietnamese-language texts of critical 4 August intercepts are not available in the public NSA archive. Hanyok notes this gap in his own study. The reconstruction of what SIGINT showed on the night of 4 August therefore rests on Hanyok's translation and interpretation of intercepts that cannot be independently verified from the public record. This is the single most important evidentiary limitation of the current verdict.

Edwin Moïse's Tonkin Gulf and the Escalation of the Vietnam War (1996) has not been fully deep-read in this research pass. As a pre-Hanyok critical academic reconstruction, it provides an independent secondary historiographical path that may contain evidence or analysis not captured in the FRUS and Hanyok paths. Full reading remains an open residual.

The exact moment the Herrick 041727Z cable reached the Oval Office or the Secretary of Defense's desk, versus when it reached the Pentagon communications centre, is not fully resolved from the available FRUS chronology. FRUS d276 records it arriving in Washington at approximately 1:27 p.m.; its journey to the principals before the 4:47 p.m. meeting and before the public address is a factual question that affects the strongest version of the personal-intent claim (C6).

North Vietnamese sources on the 4 August events — Vietnamese-language official history or military records — have not been examined in this research pass. Vietnamese official historiography has acknowledged the 2 August engagement; its account of 4 August, and whether it records any North Vietnamese naval activity that night, would add an independent national-level evidence path.

The full primary text of LBJ's 'flying fish' remark (Hanyok p.47) has not been pin-cited to a primary tape transcript or diary entry. It appears in Hanyok's study as a characterisation of Johnson's post-crisis private reaction; confirming it from a primary LBJ Library record would either strengthen or constrain its evidentiary weight.

Stockdale's negative visual observation is conveyed through Hanyok's citation of Stockdale's memoir rather than from a contemporaneous military flight report independently accessed in this research pass. Stockdale's own memoir is a primary participant account; confirming the specific language from that source would solidify this path.
wouldChange: Discovery of North Vietnamese military records confirming a 4 August attack on US destroyers, with documentation of the specific units and their engagement, would require reopening C2 and might reduce it from KNOWN to PROBABLE or less, depending on the quality and detail of such records.

A contemporaneous document — LBJ diary entry, presidential tape transcript, or memorandum — recording that either Johnson or McNamara stated awareness that no 4 August attack had occurred at the moment of the public address would upgrade C6 from POSSIBLE toward PROBABLE or KNOWN and would change the framing of the personal-intent residual throughout.

Independent access to the original Vietnamese-language texts of the critical 4 August SIGINT intercepts, allowing an independent translation and comparison with Hanyok's interpretation, would either confirm or challenge the C2 and C5 findings. If the intercepts were found to support an attack reading, C2 might be downgraded; if they confirmed Hanyok's salvage/bleed-over interpretation, C2 and C5 would be further strengthened.

Full deep-reading of Moïse (1996), if it contains evidence or analysis materially contradicting the FRUS/Hanyok reconstruction, would require incorporating that path into the evidence table and potentially revising confidence levels.

Evidence that the June 1964 draft resolution was specifically tied to a planned use of the DESOTO patrols to provoke a reaction — rather than being merely an opportunistic pre-drafted document — would upgrade C6 from POSSIBLE toward PROBABLE by strengthening the premeditation case.

Declassification of additional LBJ or McNamara contemporaneous communications from 4 August 1964 — particularly any that show awareness of the Herrick 'doubtful' cable before the public address — would bear directly on C6.

sources.name: Hanyok, Robert J. — 'Skunks, Bogies, Silent Hounds, and the Flying Fish: The Gulf of Tonkin Mystery, 2–4 August 1964,' NSA Cryptologic Quarterly (Winter 2000/Spring 2001); declassified November 2005
sources.role: The core primary source for the full-SIGINT reconstruction of the 4 August events (C2) and the SIGINT packaging findings (C5). Written by NSA historian Hanyok from full NSA archive access, including intercepts not available to outside researchers. Key page citations: p.1 (Herrick and Stockdale contemporaneous doubt); p.46–47 (June draft resolution pre-dating August; LBJ 'flying fish' remark); p.49 ('overwhelming body of reports' would have shown no attack; 'conscious effort'; 'deliberately skewed'). Inspected via the National Security Archive FOIA scan (NSA Archive EBB 132 copy). NSA portal URL frequently returns HTTP 403 for remote access; NSA Archive copy is the stable inspection path.
sources.locator: Hanyok, Robert J., 'Skunks, Bogies, Silent Hounds, and the Flying Fish: The Gulf of Tonkin Mystery, 2–4 August 1964,' Cryptologic Quarterly (Winter 2000/Spring 2001). NSA FOIA release case #43933 (2005). 56 pages. Inspected as image-only PDF via National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book 132 copy: nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB132/relea00012.pdf. Load-bearing page: p.49 (no-attack conclusion; 'fit the claim'; 'deliberately skewed'). Also available at NSA portal (access variable): nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/news-features/declassified-documents/gulf-of-tonkin/articles/release-1/rel1_skunks_bogies.pdf

sources.name: FRUS 1964–68, Volume I, Document 255 — Editorial Note: USS Maddox engagement, 2 August 1964
sources.role: The State Department's Foreign Relations of the United States documentary record of the 2 August engagement chronology. Documents the sequence: Maddox reports high-speed craft at 3:40 a.m. EDT; reports attack at approximately 4:07 a.m.; Ticonderoga aircraft assist. Primary path for C1.
sources.locator: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, Volume I, Vietnam, 1964. Document 255 (Editorial Note). Office of the Historian, US Department of State. Available at history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v01/d255

sources.name: FRUS 1964–68, Volume I, Document 276 — 4 August 1964 chronology; Herrick 041727Z; 4:47 p.m. 'marshal the evidence' meeting
sources.role: The core FRUS document for the 4 August Washington-level chronology. Records (from a 28 August reconstructed chronology): Herrick's 041727Z message at approximately 1:27 p.m. Washington time ('appear doubtful; freak weather; over-eager sonarmen; no visual sightings'); the 4:47 p.m. McNamara/Vance/JCS meeting that acknowledged 'lack of a clear and convincing showing' while concluding an attack had occurred; and the five factors cited. Primary support for C2 (same-day command doubt) and C3 (public certainty after uncertainty known).
sources.locator: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, Volume I. Document 276 (Editorial Note: Chronology of US Reaction to the Gulf of Tonkin Incidents, 2–7 August 1964, with 28 August 1964 attachment). Office of the Historian. Available at history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v01/d276

sources.name: Stockdale, James B. — airborne negative visual observation, 4 August 1964
sources.role: Admiral James Stockdale's account of flying over the Gulf of Tonkin on the night of 4 August 1964, seeing no enemy boats, no wakes, no torpedo tracks, no boat impacts — only American firepower against black sea. Documented in Hanyok p.1 citing Stockdale's memoir. An independent physical-observation path from the SIGINT and radar/sonar record. Limitation: accessed through Hanyok's citation of the memoir, not from a contemporaneous military flight report independently reviewed in this research pass.
sources.locator: Stockdale, James B., cited in Hanyok p.1: 'No boats, no boat wakes, no ricochets off boats, no boat impacts, no torpedo wakes — nothing but black sea and American firepower.' Source: Stockdale memoir (In Love and War, with Sybil Stockdale; or A Vietnam Experience). Primary: Hanyok study p.1; memoir provides the direct observation account.

sources.name: FRUS 1964–68, Volume I, Document 278 — NSC 538th Meeting, 4 August 1964 (evening)
sources.role: Record of the NSC meeting on the evening of 4 August 1964. Documents Secretary Rusk's characterisation ('unprovoked attack on the high seas is an act of war for all practical purposes'); USIA Director Carl Rowan's question ('Do we know for a fact that the North Vietnamese provocation took place?... We must be prepared to be accused of fabricating the incident'); and McNamara's response ('We will know definitely in the morning. As of now, only highly classified information nails down the incident'). Primary support for C3 (uncertainty at NSC level before public certainty claim).
sources.locator: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, Volume I. Document 278 (Summary Notes of the 538th NSC Meeting, August 4, 1964, 6:15–6:40 p.m.). Office of the Historian. Available at history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v01/d278

sources.name: Johnson, Lyndon B. — Radio and Television Report to the American People Following Renewed Aggression in the Gulf of Tonkin, 4 August 1964
sources.role: LBJ's public address announcing the second attack and retaliatory air strikes. Contains the language 'renewed hostile actions against United States ships on the high seas' and 'the initial attack on the destroyer Maddox, on August 2, was repeated today by a number of hostile vessels attacking two U.S. destroyers with torpedoes.' Primary support for C3 (public certainty language and its timing).
sources.locator: Johnson, Lyndon B., 'Radio and Television Report to the American People Following Renewed Aggression in the Gulf of Tonkin,' 4 August 1964. The American Presidency Project, University of California Santa Barbara. Available at presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/radio-and-television-report-the-american-people-following-renewed-aggression-the-gulf

sources.name: Johnson, Lyndon B. — Message to Congress, 5 August 1964 (Avalon Project)
sources.role: LBJ's 5 August message to Congress describing 'further deliberate attacks' and requesting the Resolution. Contains 'the North Vietnamese regime had conducted further deliberate attacks against U.S. naval vessels operating in international waters.' Primary support for C3 and C4.
sources.locator: Johnson, Lyndon B., Message to Congress, 5 August 1964. Avalon Project, Yale Law School. Available at avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/tonkin-g.asp

sources.name: Tonkin Gulf Resolution — PL 88-408, H.J. Res. 1145 (NARA Milestone Documents)
sources.role: The primary statutory text. Authorises the President 'to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression' and includes a Southeast Asia collective defence clause. Passed 7 August 1964. Primary support for C4 (legislative product of the dual-attack narrative).
sources.locator: Joint Resolution to Promote the Maintenance of International Peace and Security in Southeast Asia (H.J. Res. 1145), Public Law 88-408, 88th Congress, 7 August 1964. NARA Milestone Documents. Available at archives.gov/milestone-documents/tonkin-gulf-resolution

sources.name: FRUS 1964–68, Volume I, Document 280 — Leadership Meeting Notes, 4 August 1964
sources.role: Notes of the 4 August meeting with congressional leaders, at which they were briefed under the dual-attack narrative and asked to support the resolution. Primary support for C4 (congressional briefing and Resolution process).
sources.locator: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964–1968, Volume I. Document 280 (Notes of Leadership Meeting, August 4, 1964). Office of the Historian. Available at history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v01/d280

sources.name: National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book 132 — 'Tonkin Gulf Intelligence "Skewed" According to Official History,' 1 December 2005 press release
sources.role: The National Security Archive's press release and EBB 132 collection surrounding the Hanyok declassification. Not an independent evidentiary line from Hanyok — it is a curatorial layer — but provides the stable public access point for the Hanyok study and supporting documents. Quotes Hanyok's key conclusions including 'there was no second attack on U.S. ships in Tonkin on August 4, 1964' and that SIGINT 'fit the claim.' Treated as the discovery and access path, not as an independent analytical source.
sources.locator: National Security Archive, 'Tonkin Gulf Intelligence "Skewed" According to Official History,' Electronic Briefing Book No. 132, 1 December 2005. Press release and document collection at nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB132/ and nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB132/press20051201.htm

sources.name: McNamara, Robert S. — In Retrospect: The Tragedy and Lessons of Vietnam (Times Books, 1995)
sources.role: McNamara's memoir, in which he takes moral responsibility for the war's escalation but still treats the evidence for the 4 August attack as 'convincing' at the time (Hanyok p.1 note 3). The paperback edition's introduction softens some of his positions. This is a contrary participant-memory path: the Secretary of Defense centrally involved did not say in his memoir that he knew the second attack had not occurred. Used for C6 (personal intent residual) as contrary evidence.
sources.locator: McNamara, Robert S., with Brian VanDeMark, 'In Retrospect: The Tragedy and Lessons of Vietnam.' Times Books/Random House, 1995. Cited in Hanyok notes 3 and relevant passages (pp. 134–35 and paperback introduction). No stable online URL; accessible via library collections.

sources.name: Marolda, Edward J., and Oscar P. Fitzgerald — The United States Navy and the Vietnam Conflict, Volume II (Naval Historical Center, 1986)
sources.role: The official US Navy historical treatment of the Tonkin incidents, which — writing before Hanyok's declassified study — treated the second-attack evidence as conclusive. A contrary institutional lineage cited in Hanyok (note 4). Important for the independence map: official Navy history did not adopt the critical reconstruction and represents a serious institutional counter-reading, based on the same-era SIGINT products that Hanyok later concluded were selectively packaged.
sources.locator: Marolda, Edward J., and Oscar P. Fitzgerald, 'The United States Navy and the Vietnam Conflict, Volume II: From Military Assistance to Combat, 1959–1965.' Naval Historical Center, Department of the Navy, Washington DC, 1986. Cited in Hanyok note 4.

methodAudit.name: Grammar
methodAudit.note: Claims atomised into seven testable propositions. C1 (object, KNOWN): 2 August engagement occurred — factual/descriptive, primary-record supported. C2 (object, KNOWN): 4 August no attack as publicly described — careful qualifier: 'as publicly described' and 'as sold' appear throughout rather than omniscient 'nothing happened.' Loaded terms defined: 'attack (4 Aug)' means a hostile NV naval action against US destroyers that night — not radar contacts or sonar pings in isolation. 'Unprovoked' flagged as loaded public framing: DESOTO/34A context is noted throughout without using it to erase the 2 August engagement or the 4 August non-attack verdict. 'Resolution' described from statutory text, not the colloquial 'blank cheque' shorthand. 'Skewed SIGINT' attributed to the reporting-chain process level, not conflated with personal Oval Office direction. C3 and C3/C4 are separated into their distinct process claims: public certainty language; the congressional/legislative product. C5 (SIGINT packaging) is rated PROBABLE at the reporting-process level, not upgraded to proven top-down political direction. C6 (personal intent) is kept strictly separate from C2 (object-level non-attack) — a YES on C2 does not supply a YES on C6. C7 (method pair) is a logical/methodological claim, not a factual extrapolation.

methodAudit.name: Logic
methodAudit.note: Five competing hypotheses examined. H-two-attacks (both nights real as sold) rejected for night 2, supported for night 1. H-one-attack (2 Aug real; 4 Aug phantom) best supported by evidence convergence. H-fog-only (honest error only) marked as incomplete: consistent with field-operator confusion but cannot explain selective SIGINT packaging or public certainty after doubt was tabled. H-motivated (policy preference shaped evidence use) rated PROBABLE as a process companion. H-deliberate-fabrication (senior officials personally knew and lied in real time) rated POSSIBLE–PROBABLE as residual — circumstantial case exists but no contemporaneous confession and contrary memoir evidence. Hidden premises exposed: H-deliberate-fabrication requires evidence of state of mind at the moment of statement, not just evidence that doubt was available or that policy motive existed. The 4:47 p.m. 'marshal the evidence' meeting is the strongest circumstantial indicator; it is not equivalent to a document saying 'I know this is false.' Motive plus opportunity plus thin evidence raises C6 toward POSSIBLE–PROBABLE; it does not make it KNOWN. Key discrimination: 'certainty outran the evidence' (C3, KNOWN) is not the same as 'officials knowingly lied' (C6, POSSIBLE–PROBABLE). Anomaly stacking avoided: the pre-drafted resolution, the 34A raids, the DESOTO patrols, and the SIGINT selectivity are all cited at their individual evidence weight, not stacked to produce a certainty larger than any individual item supports.

methodAudit.name: Rhetoric
methodAudit.note: Standard rhetorical framings stripped. 'The Gulf of Tonkin was fake' collapses the 2 August/4 August distinction; replaced with a per-event analysis throughout. 'Johnson lied us into Vietnam' elides the fog-of-war, the multi-step reporting process, and the personal-intent gap; replaced with the claim-ledger structure that separates what the evidence supports at each level. 'The sailors were just confused' understates the selective SIGINT packaging; replaced with an explicit acknowledgement that field confusion and institutional packaging selection are distinguishable. Neutral rewrite applied: 'On 2 August 1964, US and North Vietnamese naval forces fought a real engagement in the Gulf of Tonkin. On 4 August, radar, sonar, and SIGINT reporting produced reports of a second attack while the on-scene commander was transmitting doubt. The full SIGINT record, reconstructed by NSA historian Hanyok from the complete archive, shows no second attack occurred and that the reporting process was skewed toward the attack narrative. The Johnson administration publicly described the second attack with greater certainty than the evidence warranted, before the uncertainty was resolved. The resulting Resolution was used to authorise massively expanded military commitment. Whether senior officials personally knew in real time that no attack had occurred is a finer question than the object-level finding and remains an open residual.' Identity-swap test applied: if another country's government used confused field reports and a selectively packaged intelligence product to justify a military escalation while an on-scene commander was transmitting doubt, Western historians would describe this as a serious failure of evidence and public representation — the same standard applied here.

methodAudit.name: Reality
methodAudit.note: H-one-attack generates testable predictions: contemporaneous command doubt on 4 August (confirmed, Herrick); airborne negative visual (confirmed, Stockdale via Hanyok); SIGINT reconstruction pointing to non-attack (confirmed, Hanyok p.49); no physical evidence of 4 August attack (confirmed, absence of debris/wreckage). H-motivated generates predictions: pre-existing authority desire (confirmed, June draft resolution); explicit acknowledgement of thin evidence before certainty conclusion (confirmed, 'marshal the evidence' meeting); selective SIGINT products (confirmed, Hanyok). H-deliberate-fabrication generates a prediction that fails: contemporaneous documentation of officials knowing no attack occurred (not found in available evidence). The strongest real-time documentary evidence available — the 4:47 p.m. meeting listing five factors for its conclusion — is more consistent with motivated certainty than with knowing fabrication. Controls applied: the 2 August engagement is treated as the positive control for the 4 August non-attack claim — the method must be able to distinguish the real from the phantom event, and it does.

methodAudit.name: Independence
methodAudit.note: Evidence lines counted as independence groups, not URLs. The 4 August non-attack verdict (C2) rests on three converging paths: (1) Hanyok full-SIGINT reconstruction (one NSA official history); (2) Herrick contemporaneous command doubt (one on-scene commander cable via FRUS); (3) Stockdale negative visual (one airborne observer, cited via Hanyok). These are three distinguishable paths but share one limitation: Hanyok is the primary published synthesis and also cites Stockdale — the paths are not fully independent of Hanyok's study. The FRUS chronology (d276) documenting the Herrick cable is independent of Hanyok in the sense that it is the State Department's documentary record, not NSA's. The contrary paths (Navy official history, McNamara memoir) are cited and preserved. The NSA Archive EBB 132 is correctly characterised as a curatorial layer on Hanyok, not an independent evidentiary line. Limitation explicitly noted: Hanyok's full-archive SIGINT reconstruction has not been independently replicated by another researcher with the same archive access. The original Vietnamese-language intercepts are missing from the public archive, preventing independent translation verification. These limitations are stated in C2's why field, the independence section, and the open questions.

methodAudit.name: Adversarial Pass 1 — Vietnam War historian (chronology, hindsight, simplification)
methodAudit.note: Objection: 'war started by a lie' framing is too simple — the US was already deeply involved before August 1964; the Resolution accelerated escalation, not initiation; hindsight should not be substituted for real-time complexity. Response: 'war started by a lie' language does not appear in this Evidence File; the claims are scoped to the specific August 1964 events and their public representation. C4 describes the Resolution as the legislative product, not as 'the start of the war.' Objection: DESOTO/34A context — the Maddox's connection to electronic intelligence collection and the correlated commando raids means North Vietnamese had a strategic rationale for the 2 August action. Response: DESOTO/34A context is included in the timeline and noted in C1 without using it to erase the 2 August engagement. The 'unprovoked' public framing is flagged as a loaded term in the grammar section. Objection: Hanyok is one historian using one archive; Vietnam War historians using different archives (political, diplomatic) reach different but compatible conclusions. Response: Hanyok's archive-specific expertise on SIGINT is appropriate for the SIGINT-packaging claim; the FRUS diplomatic record provides the independent chronology path. Ledger changes from this pass: none to core findings; DESOTO/34A context strengthened in C1 and timeline.

methodAudit.name: Adversarial Pass 2 — SIGINT/intelligence historian (Hanyok dependence, missing intercepts, actor attribution)
methodAudit.note: Objection: Hanyok wrote inside NSA and cannot be independently verified by outside researchers; treating one insider history as KNOWN-level evidence is too strong. Response: the independence limitation is explicitly stated in C2 and C5. KNOWN is justified by the convergence of Hanyok's reconstruction with the contemporaneous command doubt (Herrick, independent path via FRUS) and negative visual (Stockdale). If Hanyok's reconstruction stood alone, the rating might be PROBABLE. The convergence of three paths — two of which provide some independence from Hanyok — justifies KNOWN with the 'as publicly described' qualifier. Objection: missing original Vietnamese intercept texts mean the translation/interpretation cannot be verified. Response: explicitly stated as the most important evidentiary limitation in open questions; Hanyok himself notes this gap. Objection: 'deliberately skewed' is strong language; analytic culture and crisis pressure can produce selective products without deliberate intent in the sense of purposeful deception. Response: Hanyok uses this language himself; but the actor-level and mechanism question is the reason C5 is rated PROBABLE rather than KNOWN. 'Deliberately skewed' at the reporting-chain level is Hanyok's finding; the 'why' of whether it was purposeful senior direction vs. analytic-culture momentum is acknowledged as unresolved. Ledger changes: C5 kept at PROBABLE (not upgraded to KNOWN) specifically because of this pass's objection about actor-level scope.

methodAudit.name: Adversarial Pass 3 — fog-of-war defender (principals made honest error)
methodAudit.note: Objection: Steelman of pure fog-of-war — 27 radar contacts, darkness, weather, post-2-August stress, genuine belief in attack. Policymakers acted on military reports under Cold War pressure. The 4:47 p.m. meeting conclusion ('attack had taken place') reflects real decision-making under genuine uncertainty, not a knowing lie. McNamara's memoir — moral responsibility without saying 'I knew it was false' — is consistent with genuine belief at the time. Response: the fog-of-war defense is legitimate for field operators and is explicitly preserved as the strongest contrary evidence (same-night combat reports; JCS 4:47 pm conclusion; McNamara memoir residual). What it cannot fully explain: Hanyok's conclusion that the SIGINT product withheld the 'overwhelming body of reports' contradicting the attack — that selectivity required a reporting-chain process choice, not just field-level confusion. The 'marshal the evidence to overcome lack of a clear and convincing showing' language in FRUS d276 documents that the meeting started from acknowledged uncertainty, which is a stronger foundation for motivated certainty than pure fog. The fog-of-war defense helps explain how the error occurred at the field level; it has more difficulty explaining the SIGINT selectivity finding. The personal-intent question (C6) is where the fog-of-war defense is strongest, and it is why C6 stays at POSSIBLE–PROBABLE rather than PROBABLE. Ledger changes: C6 kept at POSSIBLE (not upgraded) specifically to preserve this objection's best case.

methodAudit.name: Adversarial Pass 4 — deliberate deception critic (administration knew and lied)
methodAudit.note: Objection: Steelman of deliberate deception — Herrick's cable arrived before the speech; the 4:47 pm meeting acknowledged thin evidence and then concluded attack anyway; a pre-drafted resolution was ready; Hanyok says 'deliberate skewing'; the 'flying fish' remark shows LBJ knew later, and maybe earlier. These aren't just fog-of-war — this is knowing misrepresentation. Response: the circumstantial case for C6 at PROBABLE is acknowledged: doubt was available before the speech; motivated certainty under thin evidence is documented; pre-existing authority desire is documented. What prevents PROBABLE or higher for C6: the 4:47 pm meeting still concluded attack using five listed factors — it marshalled evidence toward a conclusion but the language doesn't prove the principals knew the conclusion was false; McNamara's memoir (decades after, in a book explicitly confessing moral failure) still treats the evidence as 'convincing,' which is hard to square with a knowing same-night lie; the 'flying fish' remark is post-crisis gallows humor, not a same-night confession. A contemporaneous document recording 'I know this didn't happen' would change C6 to PROBABLE or higher. No such document exists in the available record. Ledger changes: none; the deliberate deception critic's case is absorbed into the 'would change' section as the specific type of evidence that would upgrade C6.

methodAudit.name: Adversarial Pass 5 — constitutional/congressional historian (Resolution scope, pre-existing authority, what Congress knew)
methodAudit.note: Objection: 'blank cheque' is an overstatement of PL 88-408's statutory text, which authorised 'repelling armed attacks' and 'preventing further aggression' — not open-ended war on North Vietnam. Subsequent use under executive war powers theory expanded the Resolution beyond its text. Response: 'blank cheque' language removed from C4; the actual statutory language quoted in C4. The gap between what the text authorised and what it was used to authorise is noted. Objection: not everyone in Congress was equally deceived — some senators understood the Resolution as a political signal rather than a war declaration. Response: the 88–2 vote is recorded; Morse and Gruening's dissent is noted. The claim is that Congress was briefed under the dual-attack narrative (FRUS d280), which is a factual claim about what information was presented, not a claim that every member was naive. Objection: executive war powers pre-existed the Resolution; even without it, presidents had authority to commit US forces. Response: this is a legitimate constitutional-law point acknowledged in the broader historical context. C4 is scoped to what the Resolution did and how it was used as authority, not to whether it was the only possible legal basis for escalation. Ledger changes: C4 statutory text language made more precise; 'blank cheque' characterisation explicitly qualified; Morse/Gruening dissent added to timeline entry.

changelog.change: Evidence File 006 initial publication. Research basis: private dossier passes 1 and 2 (completed by Grok AI, 2026-08-10 and 2026-08-12), independently audited and five additional hostile passes run by Claude. Sources inspected include: Hanyok NSA cryptologic history (via NSA Archive FOIA scan, key pages p.1, p.46–47, p.49); FRUS 1964–68 Volume I Documents 255, 276, 278, 280; LBJ 4 August 1964 radio/TV address (UCSB Presidency Project); LBJ 5 August message to Congress (Avalon); PL 88-408 (NARA); NSA Archive EBB 132 press (1 December 2005). Key findings: (1) 2 August engagement KNOWN — real combat, primary-record supported, must appear near top of any honest account; (2) 4 August no attack KNOWN — Hanyok full-SIGINT reconstruction, Herrick contemporaneous doubt, Stockdale negative visual; (3) public certainty KNOWN — LBJ's 'repeated today with torpedoes' language delivered after Herrick 1:27 pm cable and after 4:47 pm meeting acknowledged thin evidence; (4) Resolution KNOWN as legislative product; (5) SIGINT packaging PROBABLE at reporting-chain level, not upgraded to senior political direction; (6) personal knowing-lie by LBJ/McNamara in real time POSSIBLE–PROBABLE residual, kept strictly separate from object-level non-attack finding; (7) Northwoods/Tonkin method pair KNOWN as methodological claim; (8) five hostile-reader adversarial passes completed (Vietnam historian; SIGINT historian; fog-of-war defender; deliberate deception critic; constitutional/congressional historian) with changes recorded; (9) independence limitations of Hanyok reconstruction stated explicitly; (10) missing original Vietnamese intercepts logged as most important open residual; (11) statutory text of Resolution quoted rather than 'blank cheque' characterisation; (12) DESOTO/34A context preserved without using it to erase 2 August engagement or as argument for 4 August attack. Publication status set to public after all 18 evidence gates checked.
